data.title: Meduza: Berlin’s ‘Russian House’ stayed open despite Russia’s war in Ukraine and EU sanctions, shielded by a reciprocal deal over Moscow’s Goethe-Institut. Germany’s sabotage accusation was the final straw.
data.summary: In early September, Germany’s Foreign Ministry announced the closure of the Russian House in Berlin, Russia’s largest cultural center abroad. The center had operated in the heart of the German capital for more than 40 years. It remained open after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, even as similar institutions across Europe shut down. What finally brought it to an end was a drone attack on Leipzig Airport that German authorities described as Russian sabotage. Meduza tells the center’s story.

https://meduza.io/en/feature/2026/09/27/.label: Meduza: Berlin’s ‘Russian House’ stayed open despite Russia’s war in Ukraine and EU sanctions, shielded by a reciprocal deal over Moscow’s Goethe-Institut. Germany’s sabotage accusation was the final straw.

data.title: Meduza: A humanitarian crisis is gripping Russian-occupied Oleshky as food deliveries stop and safe evacuation becomes nearly impossible
data.summary: Oleshky (Alyoshki in Russian) is a city on the left bank of the Dnipro River, across from Kherson on the right bank. Only nine kilometers (about six miles) separate them in a straight line. People once crossed between them by bridge, but the bridge is now closed. The two cities are on opposite sides of the front: Ukraine controls Kherson, while Russia has controlled Oleshky since 2022. As in other cities near the front, life in Oleshky is difficult and dangerous. By September 2026, conditions had deteriorated so badly that people in both Ukraine and Russia were calling the situation critical. Those who remain are trying to survive without food, electricity, and adequate medical care. They cannot leave safely and often cannot even bury their loved ones. Here is what Meduza has been able to learn about conditions in the city.

https://meduza.io/en/feature/2026/09/27/.label: Meduza: A humanitarian crisis is gripping Russian-occupied Oleshky as food deliveries stop and safe evacuation becomes nearly impossible

data.title: Meduza: A decade ago, Russian airline group S7 bet on a floating spaceport to break into the commercial launch market. Yet Sea Launch hasn’t launched a rocket in more than 12 years.
data.summary: On September 27, 2016, exactly 10 years ago, S7 struck one of the most ambitious deals in Russian spaceflight: the purchase of Sea Launch, a floating spaceport designed to send commercial payloads into space from the Pacific Ocean. S7 Group had ambitious plans to capture the commercial launch market, and its CEO, Vladislav Filyov, drew comparisons to Elon Musk. Science communicator Vitaly Yegorov explains what became of the project over the next decade and how the war affected its fate.

data.title: Meduza: Dmitri Shostakovich at 120: How the icon drew on Bach, jazz, and cinema to create his own musical language
data.summary: Dmitri Shostakovich was born on September 25, 1906. Probably the most famous Soviet composer, he was forced to collaborate with the state even as he suffered under its campaign against “formalism.” For many, his life embodies the plight of an intellectual in the arts and humanities under totalitarian rule. But Shostakovich’s creative life was about far more than his fraught relationship with the authorities. At Meduza’s request, music critic Stepan Furin explores how the composer drew on classical music, jazz, and film.

data.title: Meduza: Russian street artist Slava Ptrk sums up four years abroad: ‘Unwanted There / Unwanted Here’
data.summary: One of Russia’s best-known street artists, Slava Ptrk (Stanislav Komissarov), posted an Instagram photo of a new work exploring his own experience in exile. Komissarov left Russia after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022. Russian authorities designated him a “foreign agent.” The work, “Ne nuzhen tam / Ne nuzhen tut” (“Unwanted There / Unwanted Here”), is also called “Promezhutochnye itogi chetyrekh let emigratsii” (“Four Years in Exile: An Interim Assessment”). It consists of two signs styled like bus stop signs on opposite sides of the E22 highway near Yekaterinburg, his hometown. Ptrk has reimagined urban fixtures, including road signs, in previous works. In one of his best-known works, he turned a sewer grate across from the Kremlin into prison bars. In June, another sign appeared in Yekaterinburg beneath a road sign bearing the city’s name. It read “I Miss You.”

https://meduza.io/en/feature/2026/09/28/.label: Meduza: Russian street artist Slava Ptrk sums up four years abroad: ‘Unwanted There / Unwanted Here’
